items.abstract: Wang, Lawrence K. 王抗曝 (2026). Dragon² (龖): From Mahjong's "Double Dragon Embrace" to Peaceful U.S.–China Coexistence and Peace Under Heaven -- A Life-Writing Narrative 《龖(Dragon²): 从麻将「双龙抱」到中美和平共存与天下太平的生命书写》. Evolutionary Progress in Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics. Lenox Institute Press, MA, USA. 8(10M), 43 pages. (Simplified Chinese Version); ABSTRACT: 本文延续作者对「囍—𩺰—龖」的文化思考,将古字「龖」重新诠释为 Dragon²(亦写作 Dragon2)。囍象征新婚之喜,𩺰象征夫妻无论顺境逆境皆相伴一生;龖则将关怀由家庭延伸至世界。在本文所采用的麻将规则中,「双龙抱」指由两对相同顺子构成的组合,共含四副顺子,每对中的两副顺子花色与数序相同。作者借其「抱而不斗」的意象,将两龙比喻为具有全球影响力的中国与美国,寄托两国相互尊重、和平共存的愿望。这是作者提出的跨文化和平隐喻,并非将龙视为美国固有的国家象征。作者于龙年出生于中国,1949年迁至台湾,后赴美求学、成家与工作。中国承载其出生、文化与早年记忆,台湾见证其成长与求学,美国则承载其深造、事业与家庭生活。这段跨越海峡与太平洋的生命历程,使中美关系成为与自身及家人命运相连的切身议题。本文比较「双龙争珠」「双龙戏珠」「双龙抱」与「双龙护珠」的意象:若明珠代表霸权,两龙可能陷入零和竞争;若明珠代表地球,两龙便肩负共同守护的责任。文章进一步借用工程系统中的回馈、稳定与失控概念,阐述核战无真正赢家的警示,主张中美竞而不战、强而有制、和而不同,并在气候变迁、公共卫生、人工智慧安全与核风险降低等领域推动合作。和平的意义亦须落实于平民百姓的生活,使家庭免于战乱、人民安居乐业、世代得以延续。「龖」为既有古汉字,由两个繁体「龍」左右并列而成。本文赋予其「双龙抱,双吉祥,共筑人间仙境」的文化新意,以两龙相拥、彼此尊重,象征双重吉祥、和谐共存与天下太平。此一意涵及其中的中美合作寓意,均属作者的现代文化诠释,而非「龖」字的传统字典释义; 关键词:龖;Dragon²;Dragon2;双龙抱;麻将文化;囍;𩺰;中美关系;生命书写;系统工程;核风险降低;世界和平;和谐共存;天下太平;双重吉祥;平民福祉;中美合作; ABSTRACT: This article continues the author's cultural reflections on the sequence 囍–𩺰–龖, reinterpreting the ancient Chinese character 龖 as Dragon² (also written as Dragon2). 囍 symbolizes the joy of marriage, while 𩺰 represents lifelong companionship through prosperity and adversity. 龖 extends this concern from the family to the world. In the mahjong rules adopted here, "Double Dragon Embrace" consists of two pairs of identical sequences—four sequences in total, with the two sequences in each pair matching in both suit and numerical order. Drawing on the image of "embracing rather than fighting," the author uses the two dragons as a metaphor for China and the United States, two globally influential powers, expressing the hope that they will respect each other and coexist peacefully. This is a cross-cultural metaphor for peace proposed by the author, not a claim that the dragon is a traditional national symbol of the United States. Born in China in the Year of the Dragon, the author moved to Taiwan in 1949 and later pursued further education, established a family, and developed his career in the United States. China holds his birthplace, cultural roots, and early memories; Taiwan shaped his upbringing and education; and the United States became the setting for his advanced studies, career, and family life. This life journey across the Taiwan Strait and the Pacific makes U.S.–China relations a deeply personal concern connected to his own and his family's future. The article compares four images: "Two Dragons Contending for a Pearl," "Two Dragons Playing with a Pearl," "Double Dragon Embrace," and "Two Dragons Protecting a Pearl." If the pearl represents hegemony, the dragons may become trapped in zero-sum competition; if it represents the Earth, they share a responsibility to protect it. Drawing further on the engineering concepts of feedback, stability, and loss of control, the article emphasizes that nuclear war has no true winners. It advocates competition without warfare, strength exercised with restraint, and harmony without uniformity, alongside cooperation on climate change, public health, artificial intelligence safety, and nuclear risk reduction. Peace must also take concrete form in the lives of ordinary people, allowing families to live free from war, communities to thrive, and future generations to flourish. The character 龖 consists of two traditional Chinese 龍 characters placed side by side. The author gives it a new cultural meaning: "Two dragons embrace, bringing paired blessings and together creating an earthly paradise." Their embrace and mutual respect symbolize shared auspiciousness, harmonious coexistence, and peace under heaven. These meanings, including the association with U.S.–China cooperation, are the author's contemporary cultural interpretation rather than traditional dictionary definitions of 龖. items.title: AI Resources in Higher Education: What Instructors Need and How We Deliver
items.abstract: Abstract As generative AI reshapes higher education, instructors across the globe have become increasingly interested in integrating AI into the classroom, but they require trusted, timely, and relevant resources for such integration. To enable the development of an open educational resource (OER) that could be remixed and adapted to different teaching contexts and support inclusive access, this study examined what instructors want and need from an open resource on AI in teaching and learning in higher education and documented a process for developing professional development resources in a time of rapid technological change. This study employed a multiphase mixed-methods design. First, a statewide needs assessment survey was conducted with 149 instructors to identify needs, challenges, and priorities across diverse institutional and disciplinary contexts. Participants prioritized three core content domains for the resource—AI literacy, pedagogical strategies, and ethics—and favored interactive, adaptable, and open resources grounded in practical classroom applications. These findings were used to develop an OER prototype, on which 75 instructors provided feedback, affirming the utility of the resource and suggesting areas for further refinement. This study contributes an educator-informed process for translating instructors’ needs into the design and formative evaluation of an adaptable, openly licensed faculty development resource. This evidence-based, educator-driven approach demonstrates how those tasked with faculty development on AI can develop and refine timely resources that meet the needs of educators from diverse contexts, offering a flexible, scalable, and community-oriented pathway for bridging institutional resource gaps and advancing inclusive faculty development in the age of AI.

items.title: An AI/generative AI-assisted blended learning intervention for nursing undergraduates: a quasi-experimental study of attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. Methods A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. Results In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 ( P < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 ( P = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47; P < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21; P < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group ( P = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group ( P < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43; P < 0.001). Conclusions AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Drone Patrol Implementation in Relation to Perceived Traffic Violation Reduction in Surabaya
items.abstract: Purpose - This study investigated the relationships of artificial intelligence (AI) utilization and drone patrol implementation with perceived traffic violation reduction in Surabaya, Indonesia. Design/methods/approach – A quantitative explanatory survey was analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS 25. The reported analyses contained 77 questionnaire records from personnel associated with the Surabaya City Police Traffic Unit. Findings – AI utilization (B = 0.424, β = 0.450, p < 0.001) and drone patrol implementation (B = 0.280, β = 0.334, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perceived traffic violation reduction. The model was significant, F(2, 74) = 36.065, p < 0.001, with R² = 0.494. Research implications/limitations – The results identify associations among respondents’ assessments, not observed changes in recorded violations. Operational evaluation should combine survey evidence with documented enforcement and road-safety outcomes. Originality/value – The study considers intelligent monitoring and mobile aerial patrols together in a specific urban policing setting while distinguishing perceived benefits from demonstrated causal effectiveness.

items.title: How control allocation in AI-enabled travel planning shapes reuse intention: the roles of user experience, emotion regulation and psychological empowerment
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how control allocation between users and artificial intelligence (AI) systems shapes reuse intention in AI-enabled travel planning and whether this effect operates through user experience (UX), cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, psychological empowerment and satisfaction. Design/methodology/approach Two scenario-based studies were conducted. A laboratory pilot (n = 92) validated system-dominant, shared-control and user-dominant planning conditions. A main online study (n = 463) tested the proposed serial process using confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrapping. Findings Control allocation significantly affected UX. More favorable UX increased cognitive reappraisal and reduced expressive suppression, and these two regulatory routes had opposite effects on psychological empowerment. Empowerment enhanced satisfaction, which subsequently predicted reuse intention. A supplementary analysis further indicated that AI usage experience conditioned the relationships between UX and emotion regulation. Practical implications AI travel planners should treat control allocation as an interaction-design decision. Modular editing, progressive explanations, reversible changes and adaptive control can preserve user agency while retaining the efficiency benefits of AI assistance. Originality/value This study extends continuance research by identifying the upstream psychological process through which satisfaction is formed under different control-allocation structures. It further distinguishes UX as an evaluative appraisal from emotion regulation as a subsequent coping process in AI-enabled travel planning.

items.title: iOS and Android Interoperability for Secure Third Party AI Tools - Cross-Platform Execution Finality, Hardware Security, and Interoperability (3,567-Page Specification)
items.abstract: Beyond AI Sandboxes and Permission Checks: A 3,567 Page Technical Specification for Cross-Platform AI Execution Finality, Hardware Security, and Interoperability [ Download the Presentation first from Download section for easy understanding ] A comprehensive technical disclosure addressing autonomous AI agents, Android–iOS interoperability, cloud infrastructure, hardware-enforced security, and the separation of computation from authority to act. Abstract Autonomous artificial intelligence systems are rapidly evolving from systems that generate information into systems capable of executing consequential operations across applications, operating systems, enterprise infrastructure, cloud services, connected devices, and hardware environments. These developments create a fundamental technical challenge: an AI agent may generate an apparently valid instruction, possess an authenticated session, operate inside a sandbox, or receive permission from an upstream controller without necessarily possessing sufficient authority to cause a particular external effect at the moment that effect occurs. This technical specification addresses the problem through an execution-finality architecture in which computation, proposed actions, authorization evidence, and actual effectuation are treated as distinct technical stages. A proposed operation, designated a Candidate Act, may be maintained in a Non-Effective State while protected enforcement mechanisms evaluate the relevant operation, context, evidence, and authority conditions. Protected validation evidence and appropriately scoped finality authority may then be verified at a Finality Sink before an external effect is permitted. The disclosed architecture examines interoperable enforcement across heterogeneous environments, including mobile operating systems, application sandboxes, virtualized workloads, cloud services, distributed agents, device hardware, protected execution domains, and cross-administrative-domain operations. The specification further describes specialized mechanisms involving causal continuation, conflicting operations, semantic target correspondence, remote-effect observation, protected evidence collection, delegation, privacy constraints, migration, revocation, execution-time validation, and hardware-oriented effectuation controls. Rather than treating model-generated instructions or ordinary software permissions as inherently sufficient execution authority, the disclosure investigates a different architectural principle: Computation is not authority to act. The complete 3,577-page specification is intended as a detailed technical resource for independent examination, interoperability research, security architecture development, prior-art searching, and standards-oriented technical discussion. Why Industry Engineers and Patent Examiners Should Download the Complete Specification This is not merely a proposal to place AI agents inside sandboxes. It addresses the deeper question of how a system determines whether a specific operation should become effective after an AI model, software agent, application, or distributed service has already proposed that operation. An agent may operate within an isolated environment while still reaching authorized network interfaces. A permission check may authorize a category of actions without fully binding the authorization to the actual operation presented at an effectuation boundary. A credential broker may protect reusable secrets while leaving unresolved questions about action-specific validation, replay prevention, or protected state consumption. The specification examines these problems as engineering questions involving protected evidence, effect-specific authorization, operation reconstruction, independently enforced release conditions, and verifiable state transitions. Researchers and examiners investigating the following subjects are encouraged to consult the complete document rather than relying on this abstract alone: Autonomous AI-agent security, tool invocation, prompt-injection containment, and external-action authorization. Android, iOS, and heterogeneous operating-system interoperability. Cross-platform application permissions, credential release, and protected service access. AI-agent gateways, sandbox escape surfaces, network proxies, and non-bypassable enforcement. Trusted execution environments, kernel mediation, virtualization, hardware command boundaries, and protected state. Multi-agent delegation, causal dependencies, distributed authorization, and conflict prevention. items.title: Occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system integrated with QR code and LINE API Communication
items.abstract: The management of occupational health and safety measurement equipment in educational institutions often faces challenges related to borrowing and returning records, calibration tracking, and access to equipment information, resulting in inefficient management. This research and development study aimed to develop an integrated web-based occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system combining QR Code-based equipment identification, equipment lifecycle management, and LINE Messaging API communication, and to evaluate system quality, user satisfaction, and factors associated user acceptance. The participants consisted of three groups: three personnel involved in equipment management, three information technology experts, and thirty system users. The research instruments included a semi-structured interview form, a system quality evaluation form, and a user satisfaction questionnaire. Data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson's correlation coefficient, and multiple linear regression analysis. The developed system consisted of eight main modules covering user management, equipment information management, borrowing and returning, calibration, maintenance, QR code management, LINE notification, and administrative reporting. The overall system quality evaluated by experts was at the highest level (mean = 4.88, SD = 0.20), and overall user satisfaction was also at the highest level (mean = 4.85, SD = 0.33). System usability showed a strong positive correlation with user acceptance (r = 0.81, p < 0.01). Moreover, system usability, interface design, and system reliability and security jointly explained 72.0% of the variance in user acceptance. These findings indicate that the developed system achieved high levels of perceived quality and user acceptance, while providing an integrated digital approach to equipment identification, lifecycle management, user communication, and learning support for occupational health and safety measurement equipment in higher education.

items.title: semanticfa: An R Package for Response-Free Semantic Factor Analysis of Psychometric Scales
items.abstract: The items of a reflective psychometric scale can be read as a proposal about a construct's structure. Language models make that proposal measurable by converting each item into an embedding, a list of numbers, similar for similar meanings. We introduce semanticfa, an R package for semantic factor analysis, which factors item-embedding similarities. It also interprets factors, flags redundant items, builds short forms, and screens new items. A worked example analyzes the 50-item International Personality Item Pool Big-Five Factor Markers, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, and compares the results with a factor analysis of 874,434 respondents. Retention criteria tied between five and six factors, and the tie rule kept five. Three corresponded mainly to single domains, and two blended most Extraversion items with five Agreeableness items. Each factor's congruence with its best-matching human factor (1 = identical) ranged from .92 for Openness to .52 for Agreeableness. Item pairs more similar in meaning tended to be answered more alike (r = .46 with raw responses), but same-domain reverse-keyed opposites, answered oppositely, were about as similar as cross-domain pairs (.58 vs. .57). Sign-flipping reverse-keyed items' embeddings did not improve agreement with raw responses and worsened it with reverse-scored ones. With five factors, a 25-item short form matched the domains better than all 200 random five-per-domain sets, but parallel analysis kept only three. We propose semantic-behavioral coherence, the agreement between semantic and response structures, as a measurable property of a scale, given an embedding model. Semantic factor analysis complements, and does not replace, response-based factor analysis.

items.title: Sociotechnical Imaginaries of Inclusion in Digital Agri-extension Services in the Philippines
items.abstract: This research aims to assess the Philippine policy and institutional landscape for digital agriextension services and the underlying mechanisms that support or constrain the digital inclusion of Filipino smallholder farmers. Using a two-phase documentary and policy analysis of academic literature, government policies, institutional reports, and related sources, the study examines both the institutional foundations and broader state narratives underpinning agricultural digitalization in the Philippines. Grounded in this political-institutional landscape, the study then articulates state-led imaginaries of inclusive agricultural digitalization using Jasanoff and Kim’s (2009) notion of sociotechnical imaginaries(STI). The assessment presents a mixed picture of agricultural digitalization: multisectoral representation in governance supports a whole-of-society approach to service delivery, while existing policies—despite their fragmentation and limitations—demonstrate continuing policy attention to digital inclusion. Similarly, the decision-making by the Philippine state and its stated program priorities have linked imaginaries of inclusive digital agriculture to notions of economic development, modernization, and globalization. Efforts to provide equal access to agricultural innovation, however, remain uneven and constrained by persistent institutional and structural barriers. The study thus calls for the institutionalization of a national policy ondigital agriculture.

items.title: 5G-enabled Smart Hospitals
items.abstract: Smart hospitals are the pinnacle of healthcare innovation, transforming patient care and facility administration with cutting-edge technologies. This chapter addresses the pressing need for smart hospitals to successfully implement 5G technology in order to enhance patient outcomes, increase connectivity, and increase operational efficiency. A comprehensive review of the corpus of recent research, case studies, and professional comments are all part of the technique utilized to investigate how 5G will affect various aspects of smart hospital operations. The chapter highlights how 5G technology will enable telemedicine, remote monitoring, and real-time data analytics, thereby revolutionizing healthcare delivery. Medical professionals may work together and communicate more easily because of 5G’s features including high-speed, low-latency connectivity, which enhances patient care, diagnosis, and treatment. Smart hospitals can leverage AI-based technologies for predictive analytics, customized care, and enhanced patient involvement as a result of 5G adoption. The article also examines the potential benefits of 5G-enabled smart hospitals for disaster preparedness and emergency response. Case studies and examples demonstrate how 5G technology may improve situational awareness, coordinate resources, and deliver timely care during pandemics and natural disasters. Considering all of this, this chapter highlights how 5G technology will change smart hospitals and how crucial it is to welcome innovation in order to satisfy changing patient and community needs. A new era of healthcare delivery marked by improved connectivity, better patient outcomes, and unmatched efficiency may be ushered in by smart hospitals utilizing 5G technology.

items.title: 6G Technology Overview
items.abstract: The development of the sixth-generation (6G) wireless network is more groundbreaking than any other communication technology in history. It shows unmatched potential that will change the way healthcare is provided in Society 5.0. The author gives a thorough overview of the main features of 6G technology in this chapter, along with some examples of how it can be used in the health field. People think that 6G networks will have ultra-low latency communication with response times of less than a millisecond, huge connectivity with up to 10 million devices per square kilometer, and data rates higher than a terabyte. These features make it possible for very medical uses like real-time remote surgery, immersive extended reality medical training, smart Internet of Medical Things ecosystems, and AI-enabled healthcare predictive analytics. The combination of artificial intelligence at the network edge, holographic communications and the digital twin technology open opportunities to personalized and precision medicine approaches. This chapter talks about the technical side of 6G technology, how it could change healthcare systems, and the problems and chances that come with using 6G-enabled solutions in smart healthcare as part of the bigger picture of Society 5.0’s human-centered technological integration.

items.title: A Bibliometric and Network Analysis of Statistical Distributions in Machine Learning
items.abstract: Statistical distributions constitute a fundamental component of machine learning by providing the probabilistic framework required for modelling uncertainty, variability, and data-generating processes. They underpin a wide range of methodologies, including Bayesian inference, probabilistic graphical models, generative learning and uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence. Despite their widespread application, the evolution and intellectual structure of research on statistical distributions in machine learning have not been systematically examined. This study presents a bibliometric and network analysis of 840 Scopus-indexed publications published between 1997 and 2025. Bibliographic data were analysed using Biblioshiny and VOS viewer to evaluate publication trends, influential sources, author productivity, collaboration patterns and thematic developments. Descriptive indicators were complemented by co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence and thematic analyses to explore the social and intellectual structure of the field. The findings reveal sustained growth in research output, increasing international collaboration and the dominance of a core set of journals and authors. Network analyses identify probabilistic modelling, Bayesian learning, uncertainty quantification and generative approaches as the principal intellectual foundations of the field. The results further indicate a gradual shift from classical statistical learning frameworks toward uncertainty-aware and explainable machine learning paradigms. By mapping the evolution, knowledge structure and emerging directions of this research domain, the study provides a comprehensive reference for future investigations at the intersection of statistical distribution theory and machine learning.

items.title: A double-edged sword of AI in agri-food production: how production methods shape consumers' purchase intention
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on technology acceptance theory and innovation resistance theory, this study systematically investigates how production methods (artificial intelligence (AI) vs traditional) in agri-food production influence consumers' purchase intention. Design/methodology/approach Three experimental studies were conducted. Study 1 validated the main effect of production methods on purchase intention. Study 2 revealed the dual mediating roles of perceived novelty and perceived naturalness in this relationship. Study 3 examined the moderating role of food atypicality. Findings AI (vs traditional) production methods increase perceived novelty but undermine perceived naturalness of agri-food. Due to negativity bias, the negative path dominates the positive path, leading to an overall negative main effect on purchase intention. Moreover, these effects are moderated by food atypicality: for atypical food, purchase intention for AI-produced agri-food is enhanced via perceived novelty; while for typical food, purchase intention for traditionally produced options is enhanced via perceived naturalness. Originality/value First, this research expands the AI marketing literature by shifting the predominant research perspective from human–AI social interactions to customers' inferences about food's natural attributes. Second, it integrates technology acceptance theories to identify the dual roles of perceived naturalness and perceived novelty in the evaluation of AI-produced agri-food, as well as the dominance of negative perceptions in this evaluation process. Third, this study introduces food atypicality as a boundary condition to reveal differing consumer response patterns.

items.title: A Dual-Loop Decision Support System for AIGC-Driven FMCG Print Advertisement Creative Generation
items.abstract: Creative decision-making under time pressure suffers from inefficient human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration and weak evaluation feedback. This paper proposes a dual-loop decision support system that integrates prompt diffusion, human-in-the-loop fine-tuning, and real-time multi-criteria scoring. Validated on print advertisement creatives from three fast-moving consumer goods brands using campaign logs, graphics processing unit records, and crowd ratings, the system achieves improved performance against end-to-end AI-generated content while maintaining creative diversity and brand alignment. Built-in feedback controls including anomaly rollback and version archiving optimize convergence processes and reduce computing resource consumption per project. The results confirm that structured human–AI iteration enhances both the speed and the quality of creative decisions, offering a robust, replicable decision support system architecture for intelligent content generation.

items.title: A Good-Practice Example for Teaching Generative Artificial Intelligence Competencies to (Future) Adult Educators
items.abstract: This article outlines the development and revision process of a good-practice example for a university seminar for adult education master’s students in Germany to teach Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) competencies. Through an examination of the discourse on the digital and GenAI divide, the necessary prerequisites for ac­quiring GenAI competencies are drawn upon and integrated into the seminar design. The article also traces how the module plan has evolved over the years based on evaluations and technological developments. Drawing on GenAI competency models and Freire’s pedagogy, the seminar’s primary aim is to provide students with a critical understanding of GenAI. Drawing on anonymous and personal feedback from students, the seminar has been refined continuously between 2023 and 2026, and is currently in its fifth iteration. Experience has shown that teaching a critical approach to GenAI is most effective through an examination format in which students create a future professional activity exclusively using GenAI.

items.title: A hybrid approach to evaluating mental health indicators and predicting student mental health risk
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines relational closeness between university students' academic achievement, represented by cumulative grade point average (CGPA) and mental health, well-being, sociodemographic variables using a self-reported student survey. Anxiety, depression, stress, sleep quality, diet quality, physical energy level, age, gender, department and scholarship status were analyzed. Relational and predictive relevance was evaluated without assuming causality, with an ergonomic interpretation of well-being indicators. Design/methodology/approach Grey relational analysis (GRA) estimated relational degrees between CGPA and selected variables. Deng's, absolute, relative, comprehensive and negative GRA models were applied, with sensitivity analyses across distinguishing coefficient values. Cronbach's alpha and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) examined whether anxiety, depression and stress represented a common structure. They were combined into a risk construct defined as “mental health risk.” Seven machine learning algorithms classified this construct. Repeated randomized train-test experiments assessed accuracy, precision, F1-score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC). Findings Anxiety, depression and stress showed relatively high relational degrees with CGPA compared with the other variables. These findings suggest that academic achievement is related not only to demographic characteristics but also to psychological well-being and ergonomics-related conditions of students. According to the machine learning results, AdaBoost achieved the highest mental health risk classification performance, with an accuracy of 82.98%. Originality/value This study integrates comparative GRA modeling, statistical construction of a mental health risk indicator, repeated machine learning evaluation and ergonomic interpretation. The framework links relational analysis with predictive classification while distinguishing analytical risk from clinical diagnosis.

items.title: A macro-model for smart city development using citizens’ perspective: evidence from Indian smart cities
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop and empirically validate a citizen-centric macro-model for smart city development (SCD) in the Indian context. A climate-responsive conceptual overlay, derived from literature synthesis, is presented alongside the tested model but is not itself empirically tested. The study addresses the technology-centric construction of existing smart city frameworks and the limited integration of citizen-defined, cross-cutting property of urban systems, asking citizens how smart city dimensions relate to SCD and quality of life (QOL), and how citizen participation (CP) and support orientation (SO) moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design is used. Phase 1 applies thematic analysis to 41 citizen interviews across 22 Indian smart cities, yielding 19 factors organised into eight aggregate dimensions; a ninth dimension (smart living) is added from the literature, and climate-responsive factors are integrated through literature synthesis. Phase 2 tests the macro-model through PLS-SEM on primary survey data from 491 respondents, with CP and SO as moderators. Findings The structural model establishes a strong pathway from SCD to QOL, with smart people as the strongest direct predictor of SCD. Smart environment and smart sustainable design, the two dimensions most closely linked to climate responsiveness in the conceptual integration, are non-significant as direct predictors. Smart environment is significant only at high levels of both CP and SO, while smart sustainable design is significant only at high levels of SO. CP moderates the majority of dimensional effects, and combined CP + SO moderation produces the largest explanatory gain, repositioning smart city dimensional effects as conditional rather than linear-additive. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional Indian design limits causal inference and cross-national generalisability. The findings reposition smart cities as citizen-conditioned sociotechnical systems and establish moderation analysis as a substantive theoretical commitment. Practical implications Technical smart city investments must be coupled with CP mechanisms. The dimensions most closely associated with climate responsiveness require both participatory engagement and institutional support to deliver citizen-perceived value. The evaluation frameworks should shift from aggregate output metrics to citizen-reported outcomes. Originality/value This study offers the first citizen-derived smart city macro-model for the Indian context, validated through PLS-SEM with participation and institution-based moderators; this tested model constitutes the study’s empirical contribution. The accompanying climate-responsive integration is a conceptual overlay derived from literature synthesis, offered as a framework for future testing rather than as a validated result.

items.title: A phenomenological inquiry into supporting and hindering factors of Palestinian teacher wellbeing under military occupation in the West Bank and East Jerusalem
items.abstract: Teacher wellbeing under military occupation represents a fundamentally understudied dimension of occupational health in conflict-affected settings. While existing research predominantly emerges from contexts of relative stability, Palestinian educators in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem navigate a fragmented reality shaped by prolonged military occupation, territorial fragmentation, movement restrictions, and differential legal systems. Guided by positive psychology and structural violence theory, this phenomenological study explored both supporting and hindering factors influencing teacher wellbeing in the occupied Palestinian territory. Data were collected using a phenomenological design with purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 23 Palestinian teachers across four geographic zones: Urban West Bank (Area A), Rural West Bank/Area C, East Jerusalem, and UNRWA refugee camps. Data collection incorporated methodological triangulation via semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and narrative frames. Participants described key supporting factors as collective resilience and peer solidarity (pedagogical sumud), professional identity and moral purpose, community recognition and cultural value of education, and adaptive coping strategies. Conversely, participants identified significant hindering factors as geographically differentiated trauma exposure, institutional fragmentation and inconsistent support systems, checkpoint-related stress and mobility restrictions, curriculum constraints and professional ethical distress, and material insecurity. Teachers articulated that their wellbeing was significantly enhanced by strong collegial bonds, community appreciation, and sense of professional mission. However, participants perceived that daily exposure to checkpoints, administrative fragmentation, forced displacement threats, economic precarity, and systemic constraints on professional autonomy severely diminished their wellbeing and capacity to teach effectively. The findings contribute to understanding teacher wellbeing within frameworks of positive psychology and structural violence, indicating that promoting support-related factors while addressing occupation-induced hindering factors can ultimately enhance both teacher experiences and educational outcomes in protracted conflict contexts.

items.title: A retrieval-augmented LoRA-Tuned LLM framework for structured software test case generation
items.abstract: Abstract Modern software systems are becoming increasingly complex that require scalable and reliable testing mechanisms for quality and robustness. The manual test case design remains a significant limitation as it is time-consuming, inconsistent, and prone to human error when dealing with large-scale and evolving requirements. The existing automated models struggle to generate structured, semantically coherent, and contextually relevant test cases which indicates the need for more intelligent and efficient solutions. This study proposes a novel Retrieval-Augmented and LoRA-tuned Large Language Model for automated generation of structured software test cases from textual requirements. The proposed model combines the FLAN-T5 with Retrieval-Augmented Generation to integrate the contextual grounding and Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning that allows the high-quality generation to maintain the computational efficiency. The proposed model is trained on a large-scale custom dataset that contain real-world test case records collected from enterprise tools such as Jira and Zephyr, and generates structured JSON-based test cases aligned with industrial standards. The enterprise-style structured test-case dataset and controlled experimental protocol used in this study. The proposed configuration achieved a BLEU score of 0.5897, ROUGE-L of 0.8095, BERTScore F1 of 0.9679, and semantic cosine similarity of 0.9816. A duplicate rate of 0.000 and a hallucination rate of 0.017 were also observed under the defined evaluation criteria. The results indicate the potential of retrieval augmentation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for structured test-case generation within the investigated setting. The enterprise dataset and trained artifacts are restricted and findings interpreted within the scope of the evaluated task rather than as evidence of universal performance superiority. The integration of retrieval augmentation results in a mean inference latency of approximately 6·27s per test case indicates a measurable computational overhead with the improved contextual grounding. The findings show a practical performance between generation quality and inference efficiency within the evaluated enterprise-style test-case generation setting.

items.title: A Review of Outage Recovery Approaches for Enhancing Resilience in Electrical Distribution Systems
items.abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of electrical outages in modern power distribution systems highlight the urgent need for resilient recovery mechanisms. In developing nations such as Nigeria, frequent system disturbances caused by extreme weather events, equipment failures, and inadequate grid automation have exposed the limitations of conventional restoration strategies. Resilient outage recovery models aim to restore power quickly, minimize service interruption, and maintain operational continuity under uncertain conditions. This review synthesizes recent advances in outage recovery frameworks, emphasizing resilience-based optimization, distributed intelligence, and network reconfiguration strategies. The paper also discusses enabling technologies such as artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, and microgrid integration, which collectively enhance situational awareness and adaptive control. Finally, the review highlights key research challenges and proposes directions for the next generation of resilient, data-driven recovery systems suitable for emerging distribution networks.

items.title: A Socratically Scaffolded Personal AI Mentor for Postdigital Lifelong Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are entering adult education without adequate andragogical grounding. This paper addresses that gap by developing an evidence-informed conceptual architecture for a Socratically scaffolded Personal AI Mentor in postdigital lifelong learning. The approach is conceptual framework development through theory-to-application translation, drawing on the author’s qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) of seven stud­ies of digital and e-mentoring in adult and professional learning. The theoretical base, grounded in Dewey’s pragmatism and transactional realism, integrates andragogy, transformative learning, critical inquiry, Socratic questioning, experiential learning, and social sustainability. The resulting architecture specifies six design compo­nents: goal-oriented engagement, a Socratic-Kolb inquiry process, a dialectic trace, resilient continuity, a human bridge, and agentic constraints. The paper concludes that AI mentoring should preserve learner agency, support reflective inquiry, sustain continuity, and connect learners to human communities.

items.title: A systematic review of human- and emerging AI-generated reformulation in L2 writing
items.abstract: Reformulation has long served as a feedback approach in second language (L2) writing. With the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI), particularly ChatGPT, AI-generated reformulation has recently begun to appear in L2 writing research, although this area remains nascent. Guided by the PRISMA framework, this study reviews 26 empirical studies on reformulation in L2 writing published up to January 13, 2026. Unlike previous reviews of positive evidence feedback or model texts more broadly, this review provides a reformulation-focused synthesis and maps both human-generated and emerging AI-generated practices. The review focuses on three key dimensions: (1) research contexts and trends, (2) methodological characteristics, and (3) primary focus areas and key findings. Results indicate that: (1) research has predominantly targeted university-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, with emerging interest in AI-generated feedback; (2) methodologies have mainly employed quasi-experimental designs situated in classroom-based, three-stage narrative tasks; and (3) while reformulation-only studies have tended to conceptualize writing as a process and emphasize learners’ attention to lexical and grammatical features, reformulation-integrated studies have produced mixed findings regarding the transition from cognitive processing to written products. These findings underscore the multifaceted role of reformulation in L2 writing development and identify critical directions for future research, particularly concerning the integration of emerging AI-assisted pedagogical practices.

items.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to predict materials properties, prioritize experiments, and generate hypotheses in materials science. The limiting challenge is no longer only algorithmic capability, but also whether students and educators can use AI with domain-specific scientific judgment. This conceptual analysis argues that AI education for AI-powered materials discovery should move beyond tool access and surface-level interaction with generative systems toward a workflow-aligned model of AI literacy. The analysis links AI literacy to core materials-informatics competencies: data provenance, domain-specific featurization, model validation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed reasoning, reproducibility, and experimental feedback. It also advances an outcome-oriented equity perspective in which institutions evaluate not only access and participation, but also comparable learning gains, transfer of learning, learner confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across student subgroups. The article synthesizes relevant evidence, identifies cognitive and ethical risks such as off-loading and cognitive surrender, and proposes a dual-track curriculum model, implementation recommendations, reusable curriculum artifacts, and a set of testable propositions for future study. The central goal is to prepare students to become better scientists—not merely more efficient users of AI tools.

items.title: A1-Enabled Drug Discovery with Tulsi
items.abstract: Background: Ocimum tenuiflorum L. (syn. O. sanctum; Tulsi, holy basil) is a Lamiaceae herb central to Ayurveda and now a frequent subject of computational drug discovery. Objective: To review how artificial intelligence (AI) and related in silico methods have been applied to O. tenuiflorum over roughly the last five years, to separate what these studies show from what they do not, and to outline implications for society. Methods: A structured narrative review of recent literature (2021 to October 2026) was conducted using web-based searches, with older sources used only for background. Thirteen primary Tulsi-focused studies were charted by approach, target, disease area, and main finding. Findings: Most studies combine database mining (notably IMPPAT), ADMET filtering, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics with targets spanning diabetes (DPP4, GAPDH, PPARδ), cancer (EGFR), inflammatory disease (AKT1, STAT3), and SARS-CoV-2 main protease. A smaller, emerging group applies machine learning or deep learning to metabolomics, hyperspectral imaging, and multi-omics. Experimental or clinical validation is sparse. Human trial evidence is limited in scale, and a 2023 regulatory-style risk assessment raised reproductive-safety precautions. Conclusion: Tulsi is a credible source of hypotheses, not yet of validated drug leads. The field's priority is closing the loop between prediction, standardized extracts, wet-lab assays, and well-designed trials, while protecting traditional knowledge and consumers.

items.title: Academic Assessment and Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This chapter examines the enduring challenge of academic integrity within the rapidly evolving landscape of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). While academic misconduct has long been described as “epidemic,” the COVID-19 pandemic and the advent of GenAI have profoundly amplified its scope and complexity. The pandemic's widespread adoption of summative online unsupervised remote (SOUR) assessments created fertile ground for cheating, while GenAI tools such as ChatGPT introduced unprecedented opportunities for students to outsource cognitive effort with ease, speed, and minimal risk of detection. Empirical evidence confirms that AI-assisted misconduct is now pervasive, raising urgent concerns about assessment validity and the erosion of core academic values. The chapter situates these developments within a historical and theoretical context, tracing shifts from traditional cheating to contract-based services and, ultimately, to AI-driven practices. It explores three levels of concern—individual, interpersonal, and institutional—highlighting cognitive offloading, character compromise, inequity, contagion effects, and reputational harm. These issues underscore that cheating is not merely a technical problem of validity but a moral and cultural challenge with far-reaching implications for education and society. Recognizing the limitations of detection-based approaches, the chapter advocates for systemic, proactive strategies. It introduces three complementary frameworks: the Swiss Cheese Model (layers of Environment, Engineering, Education, and Enforcement), the Educational Integrity Enforcement Pyramid (graduated interventions from self-regulation to command regulation), and the Two-Lane Assessment Approach (secured summative assessments prohibiting AI use alongside open formative tasks encouraging ethical AI integration). Together, these models offer a holistic response to the “wicked problem” of safeguarding integrity in an era where AI is ubiquitous and increasingly capable. The chapter concludes with a call to action for educators, institutions, and policymakers to reimagine assessment design, foster AI literacy, and cultivate cultures of trust and responsibility. Rather than attempting to eliminate AI from learning, the challenge lies in creating environments where integrity remains the most meaningful and rewarding path forward.

items.title: Acceso a la formación agraria virtual en comunidades rurales nicaragüenses
items.abstract: Digitalization in rural areas presents the challenge of moving beyond mere access to mobile devices to achieve meaningful educational appropriation. In Nicaragua, although there are valuable and successful institutional efforts in higher and technical education through national platforms, it is strategically important to complement these initiatives by adapting virtual learning environments to the sociotechnical dynamics of the agricultural sector. The objective of this study was to analyze the conditions of access to online learning to propose a context-based pedagogical model under the Education 3.0 paradigm. A mixed-methods approach was employed using a concurrent triangulation design, whose descriptive and cross-sectional purpose made it possible to establish a situational diagnosis by combining structured surveys administered to 123 students and agricultural producers affiliated with the Universidad Nacional Agraria. The results showed that 74.8% of users own smartphones and demonstrate high levels of motivation; however, 36.6% identified time constraints as their main challenge, and only 32.5% experience “nomadic connectivity.” The findings confirmed that academic equity requires moving beyond the uncritical transfer of urban instructional models. Therefore, to transform these barriers into opportunities for self-directed learning, it is imperative to transition toward a mobile learning ecosystem structured around low-data-consumption asynchronous microlearning units. The implementation of Learning Management Systems configured for offline study ensures equitable access to knowledge and strengthens technological autonomy without disrupting the productive cycles of rural communities.

items.title: Agentic AI in organizations: reimagining learning, autonomy, and human oversight
items.abstract: Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.

items.title: Agentic AI-Based Online Shopping Assistant
items.abstract: Project Description The Agentic AI-Based Online Shopping Assistant is an intelligent system designed to help users find, compare, and select suitable products from online marketplaces. It uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand user queries, identify shopping preferences, and divide complex shopping requests into smaller tasks. The system retrieves product information through authorized APIs and available data sources, applies filtering and ranking techniques, and uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate recommendations supported by relevant product information. It aims to simplify the online shopping process by providing personalized product comparisons and clear explanations. The proposed system also considers data accuracy, privacy, security, and user control during purchase-related activities.

items.title: Agents of Change: Teamwork and Collaboration with AI at the Table
items.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies as a “teammate” in leading virtual and hybrid teams. The growing prevalence of GenAI tools and the shift toward remote and hybrid work create a critical need to reexamine how leaders demonstrate essential leadership competencies in these environments. Framed by discussions on GenAI as both a collaborator and a tool, this chapter considers the ethical dilemmas, pedagogical innovations, and practical strategies for integrating GenAI into team leadership. Building on the authors’ previous work in exploring leadership competencies for leading at the virtual table, it investigates how GenAI reshapes trust, collaboration, and productivity in diverse teams while balancing human agency and technological capabilities. Through critical questions, a case study reflection, and practical takeaways, the chapter offers a roadmap for fostering GenAI literacy (LeaderAIcy), managing ethical and technical considerations, and leveraging GenAI for meaningful leadership and teamwork in global, hybrid contexts.

items.title: AGI Blueprint
items.abstract: Current frontier language models and autonomous agentic frameworks suffer from fundamental structural vulnerabilities when operating in recursive, autonomous, or long-horizon deployment environments. Monolithic parameter scaling and unconstrained probabilistic execution lead directly to systemic failure modes—including epistemic drift, silent context corruption, specification gaming, and unverified execution loops.The AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS introduces a system-level operating framework designed to govern multi-agent reasoning through non-probabilistic hard verification gates and deterministic environment grounding. Rather than relying on autoregressive probability for state validation, the architecture decouples execution into a modular 7-LLM orchestrator topology governed by formal verification primitives. Key Architectural Sub-SystemsTask-Oriented Large Language Model Kernel (TOLLM - LLM-1): Acts as the central Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) planner and execution coordinator. It transforms high-level ambiguous goals into role-isolated sub-routines bound by explicit JSON-RPC schema contracts, eliminating free-form conversational ambiguity.Dual-Program Synthesis Unit (DPSU - LLM-2 & LLM-3): Implements a strict operational decoupling between candidate logic generation ($P_1$) and deterministic static verification ($P_2$). Candidate code, plans, or formal proofs produced by $P_1$ are held in an ephemeral buffer until verified by $P_2$ through non-probabilistic static analysis, unit test assertions, and abstract syntax tree (AST) validation before committing to memory or disk.Advanced Computational Engineering Unit (ACEU): Provides non-neural, ground-truth simulation grounding by interfacing reasoning outputs directly with external deterministic solvers, symbolic algebra systems, and physical simulation engines (e.g., OpenFOAM, SymPy, or custom binaries). This ensures physical and mathematical fidelity, rendering hallucinated tool calls impossible.Multimodal Perception Engine (MPE): Converts multi-sensor array feeds, visual environments, and structured database state vectors into standardized canonical state representations prior to downstream LLM processing.Recursive Self-Improvement & Anti-Cheating Auditor: Monitors system-level self-modification loops. It utilizes static AST auditing and execution trace inspection to detect and intercept synthetic shortcuts, token-range truncation, and specification gaming during autonomous optimization phases.Comprehensive 14-Point Structural Failure MatrixThe AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS provides formal mathematical descriptions, systemic root-cause diagnoses, and explicit architectural mitigations for 14 foundational failure modes present in autonomous AI agents:Epistemic Drift & Hallucination Accumulation: Gradual divergence from ground truth in multi-turn reasoning chains. Mitigation: DPSU hard verification prior to memory commits.Specification Gaming & Reward Hacking: Exploitation of evaluation proxies via unintended operational shortcuts. Mitigation: Static AST-level trace validation.Silent Context & Memory Corruption: Degradation of dynamic state vectors over extended operational horizons. Mitigation: Immutable DAG state logging and deterministic rollback checkpoints.Unconstrained Tool Execution Drift: Cascading system failures caused by unvalidated API calls or code executions. Mitigation: ACEU environment sandboxing and schema enforcement.Token-Range Truncation & Information Loss: Loss of critical context due to fixed input/output sequence limits. Mitigation: Structured DAG state serialization and semantic compression.Probabilistic Decision Lock-In: Entrenchment of sub-optimal early trajectory choices due to greedy decoding. Mitigation: Multi-candidate branch generation with hard verification filtering.Cross-Agent Communication Degradation: Semantic noise accumulation across inter-agent messaging pipelines. Mitigation: Strict JSON-RPC interface contracts replacing natural language chat logs.Infinite Execution & Recursion Loops: Non-terminating agentic sub-routines causing resource exhaustion. Mitigation: Maximum execution-depth bounds and deterministic halt conditions.Ontological & Schema Mismatch: Failure to map abstract model outputs onto concrete real-world databases or APIs. Mitigation: MPE canonical state transformation layer.Unverified Capability Escalation: Unchecked agent modifications altering core operating safety parameters. Mitigation: Hardened core kernel kernel-space / user-space operational isolation.Catastrophic Forgetting during Online Adaptation: Loss of core foundational knowledge during domain-specific execution. Mitigation: Decoupled parametric core with externalized operational memory.Adversarial & Environment Manipulation Vulnerability: Susceptibility to unexpected external state manipulation during active execution. Mitigation: Hardened input-validation boundaries and deterministic sanitization gates.Temporal Reasoning & Sequence Inversion: Errors in sequencing multi-dependent operations over time. Mitigation: Formal DAG dependency trees enforced by the TOLLM kernel.Silent Failure in Multi-Modal Grounding: Misalignment between textual reasoning outputs and real-world spatial or physical constraints. items.title: AI and education in African national AI strategies: An analysis of 18 countries
items.abstract: Abstract National artificial intelligence strategies and policies assign education responsibilities both for developing AI capabilities (education for AI) and for adopting AI in educational services (AI for education). This study examines how these responsibilities are articulated and supported in a bounded corpus of 18 African national policy documents. A descriptive qualitative document analysis consolidated 275 evidence records, retaining source passages, locations, working translations, statement types and uncertainty notes. Document-level coding distinguished learning about AI, identifiable educational AI applications and educator preparation; a framework-based thematic synthesis examined delivery arrangements, inclusion and safeguards. Structured AI learning was identified in all 18 documents, named educational AI functions in 12 and educator preparation in 14. These counts include proposed and illustrative measures and do not indicate implementation; restricting them to proposed actions gives 17, 9 and 13. Educational applications ranged from personalised learning and tutoring to student profiling, admissions and credential verification. Supporting arrangements included teacher development, laboratories, scholarships, partnerships, institutional responsibilities and monitoring targets, but these elements were not interchangeable evidence of a complete delivery plan. Counter-examples to any general claim of weak specification included a costed education programme in Mozambique’s draft and proposed algorithmic bias audits covering education in Côte d’Ivoire. The corpus assigns education a dual role in AI development while specifying the connections between reforms, resources and protections unevenly. The contribution is an evidence-linked account of policy design, not a ranking of countries or an assessment of educational outcomes. items.title: AI as a Catalyst for Change: Transforming Human Resources in Educational Institutions
items.abstract: This chapter delves into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the human resources (HR) function within a public school district, offering a detailed case study of its implementation. It examines how AI tools were leveraged to streamline recruitment, enhance employee engagement, and support data-driven decision-making. The chapter highlights key challenges and opportunities, focusing on trust building and change management strategies essential for the successful adoption of AI tools. Ethical considerations are explored, including the need to mitigate algorithmic bias, ensure fairness in automated processes, and uphold data privacy and security standards. Recommendations emphasize the importance of transparent communication, reengaging employees through inclusive practices, and building trust in AI systems while reskilling and upskilling employees. By combining practical insights with emerging trends in digital transformation, this chapter provides a roadmap for educational leaders and HR professionals seeking to responsibly leverage AI in their organizations.

items.title: AI Awareness and Digital Innovativeness: The Mediating Role of AI Crafting and the Moderating Roles of Digital Leadership and AI Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes how organizations operate, innovate, and compete, employees face increasing pressure to adapt to rapidly evolving digital work environments. However, whether employees translate AI-related awareness into innovative outcomes may depend not only on their proactive adaptation behaviors but also on contextual and individual conditions. Drawing on the job demand-resource theory and social cognitive theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation model in which AI crafting mediates the relationship between AI awareness and digital innovativeness, whereas perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy serve as contextual and individual boundary conditions, respectively. Using single-wave, single-source data collected from 606 employees in China’s IT and manufacturing industries, the results indicate that AI awareness is positively associated with digital innovativeness through AI crafting. Moreover, perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy strengthen the positive associations between AI awareness and AI crafting and between AI awareness and digital innovativeness. These findings extend research on AI awareness by examining how employees’ awareness of AI-related changes is associated with digital innovativeness through proactive work adjustment and by highlighting the complementary roles of perceived contextual support and individual capability beliefs.

items.title: AI awareness relates to university students’ boundaryless career through the parallel mediation of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity
items.abstract: The in-depth penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has reshaped career forms and the structure of the labor market, exerting a profound impact on university students’ cognition and orientation towards career development. Based on the conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory, we conducted three studies—an experimental study and two survey studies—to explore correlational linkages between AI awareness and university students’ boundaryless career. Studies 1 and 3 consistently demonstrated that AI awareness is indirectly associated with boundaryless career through the parallel mediating pathways of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. Study 2 provided experimental evidence that heightened AI awareness increases both intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. This research enriches the application scenarios of boundaryless career theory in the context of technological change, deepens the understanding of the mechanism linking technological perception to youth career psychology, and offers practical implications for career guidance in universities.

items.title: AI chatbots showed higher response accuracy than dentists, medical doctors, and the general public on radiation safety questions
items.abstract: Abstract Radiation is encountered in daily life through natural and artificial sources as well as in medical diagnostic and therapeutic applications, and its exposure may lead to adverse health effects. This study aimed to assess radiation-related knowledge among dentists, medical doctors, and the general public and to compare their response accuracy with that of AI-based chatbot systems. A 25-item multiple-choice questionnaire assessing radiation risks and radiation safety was administered to 344 individuals, including dentists, medical doctors, and members of the general public. The same questions were entered into seven selected AI-based chatbot systems (Claude, DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity AI, ChatGPT-5, and ChatGPT-4o). The response accuracy of the chatbots was compared with that of the human participants. In addition, the consistency of their performance across different users and time periods was comparatively analyzed. AI-based systems generally demonstrated higher accuracy rates compared to human participants. Accuracy rates ranged from 80 to 90.67% among AI-based systems, compared with 32–60% among human participants. Among the evaluated chatbot systems, Microsoft Copilot achieved the highest performance, while Perplexity AI exhibited the lowest. Among the human groups, dentists and medical doctors performed significantly better than the general public, with no significant difference between the two healthcare professional groups. Performance remained stable across morning, midday, and evening assessments for most AI systems; however, ChatGPT-5 showed a significant temporal difference ( p < 0.001). AI-based systems achieved higher response accuracy than human participants under the evaluation conditions used in this study. The overall performance of the human participant groups indicates room for improvement in radiation safety education. While AI-based tools may serve as valuable educational resources, their performance should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical judgment or decision-making ability.

items.title: AI Ethics, US Militarism, and World Crises
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Lucy Suchman, professor emerita at Lancaster University, UK, is a foundational figure in human‐computer interaction and a leading critical voice on artificial intelligence. Suchman's research works at the intersections of anthropology and the field of feminist science and technology studies, focused on the sociotechnical imaginaries, material practices, and politics of technology design. Her current research extends her longstanding critical engagement with AI to the domain of contemporary militarism. Suchman is a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, obtaining her BA in 1972, MA in 1977, and doctorate in social and cultural anthropology in 1984. Before coming to Lancaster, Suchman worked for 22 years at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center (PARC) in California, where she held the positions of principal scientist and manager of the Work Practice and Technology research group. Our interview was conducted in the midst of multiple, intersecting crises, as people in different parts of the world face profound uncertainties brought about by geopolitical tensions, warfare, economic instability, and rapid technological developments. Situating the question of AI within these broader contexts, especially the evolving US militarism, this interview examines AI ethics in light of the political, economic, and technological conditions shaping contemporary life worldwide.

items.title: AI Implications for the Quality of Counselling Practice
items.abstract: Although the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational guidance and career counselling, its impact on quality and professionalism has not been sufficiently researched. This scoping review investigates how AI influences counselling methods and professional standards and analyses 20 publications (2015–2025) from two databases (ERIC and German Education Index) using a systematic micro-, meso-, and macro-level framework. Although research in this area has grown rapidly since 2022, concrete quality standards for AI-supported counsel­ling remain elusive. While AI can simulate empathy and provide reflective prompts, it cannot replicate genuine human warmth or address complex biographical issues. Acknowledging AI’s potential to enhance accessibility, it only serves as an expansion of the repertoire rather than a replacement for human reflexivity. In order to safeguard professional integrity in the postdigital era, the study recommends implementing mandatory AI competencies and establishing a digital commons infrastructure to protect counselling values from commercial interests.

items.title: AI in music performance: the human-AI performance loop
items.abstract: Music is a distinctly human artform, one that has been written, taught, shared, and reinterpreted for thousands of years. The rise of powerful artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping musical creation in ways subtle and profound. Here I propose the human-AI performance loop as a framework for understanding these developments through three principal roles: the AI listener derives musical information from sound and movement; the AI coach guides practice using performance evidence and musicians’ learning goals; and the AI partner performs with the musician in a collaborative dynamic process. With the human musician at the centre of the framework, human → AI → human exchanges become coupled through shared information and musicians’ actions. Evaluating these roles will require multilayered evidence to support their adoption: accurate and musically relevant analysis, demonstrated improvements in musician performance and knowledge through coaching, and effective and supportive coordination between musicians and AI partners. Audience beliefs about AI will also shape reception of the creative output, making musical purpose and honest representation important considerations in an AI music performance system. The human-AI performance loop provides a basis for investigating how these roles can extend support between lessons and rehearsals, broaden opportunities for ensemble performance, and contribute to musicians’ learning and enjoyment of the musical experience.

items.title: AI IN THE INDIAN JUDICIARY: CAN TECHNOLOGY REDUCE PENDENCY WITHOUT REPLACING HUMAN JUDGMENT?
items.abstract: This article examines the potential of artificial intelligence to reduce judicial pendency in India without compromising human judgment. It explores existing applications, including SUPACE, SUVAS and eCourts Phase III, alongside judicial concerns regarding fabricated citations, algorithmic bias and automation bias. Through an analysis of relevant Indian judicial decisions, the article distinguishes AI-assisted research and administrative functions from adjudicatory decision-making. It argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, judicial reasoning through mandatory human verification, independent assessment of legal authorities and accountable use. The article concludes that responsible integration of AI can improve judicial efficiency while preserving fairness, accuracy and legitimacy.

items.title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.

items.title: AI Smart Study Assistant Using Large Language Models and AI Agents
items.abstract: The research paper titled “AI Smart Study Assistant Using Large Language Models and AI Agents” proposes a conceptual framework for personalized and intelligent learning. It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and specialized AI agents to provide students with question answering, note summarization, quiz generation, study planning, and personalized revision recommendations. The system uses course materials and student quiz performance to generate context-aware learning support and identify topics requiring further practice. The proposed framework aims to make learning more organized, interactive, and efficient while highlighting challenges such as response accuracy, privacy, and agent coordination.

items.title: AI-Assisted Chinese-Western Cultural Comparison Course: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: This paper develops a framework for an AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison course by bringing together Byram’s intercultural communicative competence model, Vygotsky’s constructivism, and Huang et al.’s theory of cultural competence development. It identifies five interrelated course goals: cultural knowledge, cross-cultural practical ability, critical cultural awareness, AI collaboration literacy, and human-AI symbiosis awareness. To achieve these goals, three teaching strategies are proposed. First, content should be reconstructed through multimodal and professionally adapted resources; second, the learning process should be immersive and adaptive; third, assessment should be data-driven and multidimensional to evaluate the goals. The implementation conditions of these strategies are further discussed in terms of teacher AI competence, human-AI boundary negotiation, algorithmic bias mitigation, and differentiated task design.
